# Arterial access

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Anesthesiology > Arterial access*

[Original Article Link](/library/aF0Qg3)

---

## Summary

Arterial access may be required for <u>arterial blood gas</u> (<u>ABG</u>) sampling, <u>arterial line insertion</u>, or as an entry point for other endovascular procedures (e.g., <u>coronary angiography</u>). <u>ABG sampling</u> is commonly performed by puncturing the radial or <u>femoral artery</u>. An <u>arterial line</u> may be placed for continuous blood pressure monitoring or frequent <u>ABG sampling</u>. Contraindications include inadequate circulation, <u>Raynaud syndrome</u>, <u>thromboangiitis obliterans</u>, and <u>full thickness burns</u>. Prior to arterial access, an appropriate site should be selected (most commonly the <u>radial artery</u>) and necessary equipment should be brought to the bedside. Complications include bleeding, <u>AV fistula</u> formation, <u>hematoma</u> formation, and <u>pseudoaneurysm</u>.




See “<u>ABG analysis</u>” for the interpretation of <u>ABG</u> findings.

---

## Definitions

* <u>Arterial blood gas</u> (<u>ABG</u>) sampling: arterial blood drawn for the purposes of <u>ABG analysis</u>, typically from the <u>radial arteries</u> or an indwelling <u>arterial catheter</u>.

* Arterial line: an indwelling catheter that enters via the <u>skin</u> and terminates within an <u>artery</u> (e.g., the <u>radial artery</u>)

---

## Preparation

### Common puncture sites




* <u>ABG sampling</u>: radial, brachial, and <u>femoral arteries</u>

* <u>Arterial line</u>: radial and <u>femoral arteries</u>





### Modified Allen test




#### Clinical applications




* May be performed prior to <u>radial artery puncture</u> to assess collateral circulation in the hand.

* Not routinely recommended for single <u>radial artery puncture</u>.  [[2]](/library/3wYSir)[[3]](/library/tI1XeR0)

* An abnormal result is suggestive of inadequate collateral blood flow; consider an alternative puncture site.





#### Steps



1. * The patient elevates their hand and makes a tight fist.
2. * Apply pressure to the radial and <u>ulnar arteries</u> to occlude <u>palmar</u> <u>perfusion</u>.
3. * Release pressure from the <u>ulnar artery</u> as the patient releases their fist.
4. * Observe the palm for 15 seconds:

* Normal: The palm becomes flushed within 5 seconds.

* Abnormal: The palm remains pale for 5–15 seconds.




![Modified Allen test](media/j0bwewjgqmwm94qlmz4wxv2q.jpg)

Modified Allen test

![Modified Allen Test - Clinical Examination](media/small_607556ec4d50b.jpg)

## Technique/steps

The following applies to adults.




### Radial artery puncture



1. * Obtain <u>informed consent</u>.
2. * Position the wrist in mild <u>dorsiflexion</u>
3. * <u>Prep the skin</u>; create a <u>sterile field</u> if <u>arterial line insertion</u> is indicated.
4. * Consider securing the wrist with tape.
5. * Locate the <u>radial artery</u> using either palpation or <u>ultrasound</u> guidance.
6. * Consider <u>single point local anesthesia</u> for the <u>skin</u> above the insertion site.
7. * Puncture the <u>skin</u> with the needle at a 30–45° angle to the <u>skin</u>.
8. * Advance the needle along the course of the pulsating <u>artery</u> until <u>blood flashback</u> is observed.
9. * Continue steps for <u>ABG sampling</u> or <u>arterial line insertion</u> as required.




![Radial artery ultrasound (1/2)](media/evc72axuumhf40e2f8elcs7m.jpg)

Radial artery ultrasound (1/2)

![Radial artery ultrasound (2/2)](media/rda77qw5murg5e2ihmwiqral.jpg)

Radial artery ultrasound (2/2)




### ABG sampling from the <u>radial artery</u>  [[2]](/library/3wYSir)



1. * Follow steps for <u>radial artery puncture</u> using a bevel-up needle.
2. * Once <u>blood flashback</u> is visible, allow the syringe to fill on its own.
3. * Remove the needle and apply firm pressure to the puncture site for 3–5 minutes.
4. * Remove excess air from the syringe by gently depressing the plunger and place an end cap.




![Radial artery puncture with arterial blood gas (ABG) sampling](media/m8xas7pbd6qrwujhwuwissdx.jpg)

Radial artery puncture with arterial blood gas (ABG) sampling




### Radial arterial line insertion




The technique for <u>arterial line placement</u> depends on the site selected and the equipment available and is performed under sterile conditions.




#### <u>Arterial catheter</u> with a built-in guidewire




The Arrow® kit is an example of a commonly used device for this purpose.



1. * Follow steps for <u>radial artery puncture</u> using the needle-guidewire-catheter assembly.
2. * Once <u>blood flashback</u> is observed, stabilize the needle and advance the guidewire into the vessel using the wire guide handle.
3. * Advance the catheter over the wire into the vessel.
4. * While removing the needle and guidewire, apply occlusive pressure over the <u>proximal</u> <u>artery</u> to avoid blood loss.
5. * Attach the pressure transducer tubing to the catheter.
6. * Secure the catheter with sutures and apply a <u>sterile dressing</u>.




![Arterial catheter placement](media/o9gqe08nos2tr9cy1uez95on.jpg)

Arterial catheter placement




#### Direct over-the-needle technique (no guidewire)



1. * Follow steps for <u>radial artery puncture</u> using the available needle-catheter assembly.
2. * Once <u>blood flashback</u> is observed, advance the catheter over the needle into the <u>artery</u>.
3. * While withdrawing the needle, apply occlusive pressure over the <u>proximal</u> <u>artery</u> to avoid blood loss.
4. * Attach the pressure transducer tubing to the catheter.
5. * Secure the catheter in place with sutures and apply a <u>sterile dressing</u>.
